summary: Learners (ages 11–13) name the seven components of a healthy diet — carbohydrates, lipids (fats and oils), proteins, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water — give a food source for each, and state its body role. The central discrimination is which components are the main energy providers (carbohydrates and lipids, with protein a secondary or backup energy source whose main job is growth and repair) versus which provide no or very little energy (vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre, which our own enzymes cannot digest). Activities move learners from 'healthy vs junk food' folk categories to a functional account where each nutrient does a specific job and 'balance' means right proportions, not eliminating any group.
misconceptions: Believing vitamins and minerals provide energy (they do not).
Thinking all fat is unhealthy and should be eliminated, rather than being a needed energy store.
Assuming protein is only for athletes/muscle-building rather than for all growth and repair.
Treating fibre and water as unimportant because they carry no energy.
Equating 'healthy diet' with eating less, rather than eating the right balance.

activities.title: Nutrient job cards: source, role, and energy tag
steps: For each of the seven nutrients — carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water — write or state one food source, the job it does in the body, and whether it provides energy.

Sort the seven nutrients into two groups: 'main energy providers' (carbohydrates, lipids; protein as a secondary or backup source whose main job is growth and repair) and 'no or very little energy' (vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre, which our own enzymes cannot digest).
Answer two myth-busting prompts explicitly: 'Do vitamins give you energy?' and 'Is all fat bad?', explaining your reasoning in a sentence each.

Optionally use a balanced-plate illustration where tapping a food reveals its nutrient card (e.g. tap chicken → 'protein — building blocks for growth and repair'; tap oil → 'lipid — concentrated energy store and insulation'), with a colour/icon key tagging energy vs non-energy groups and a lift-the-flap reveal for the two myth questions.
activities.insight: Each nutrient has a distinct job, and only some nutrients supply energy; a healthy diet fills all seven jobs in the right proportions rather than sorting foods into 'good' and 'bad'.

activities.title: Build a balanced plate
steps: Assemble a meal by choosing foods for a plate, aiming for the right proportions across the seven nutrient groups rather than maximising any single one.
Watch a live feedback panel (e.g. seven nutrient bars that fill as foods are added) and adjust the meal so no group is overloaded or missing.
Explain in one or two sentences why your finished plate counts as 'balanced' — which groups are present and roughly in what proportion.
activities.insight: 'Balance' is felt as proportion across all seven jobs, not as eliminating a food group or eating less overall.

activities.title: Food-energy investigation (supervised)
steps: Before testing, PREDICT which of two equal-mass foods will heat water more and why — e.g. a crisp (or a peanut only if no one present has a nut allergy), which is fatty/starchy, versus a grape or lettuce leaf.

Under adult supervision, burn an equal mass of each food at the same distance beneath a boiling tube holding the same volume of water at the same starting temperature, and measure the temperature rise; then repeat with the second food. Very watery foods such as grape or lettuce may barely burn, and that result itself reflects their high water content and low energy per gram.
Compare the measured temperature rises to your predictions and explain what the result shows about where dietary energy sits.

Answer the probing questions: which two of the seven components give most of your energy and which give little or none; if vitamins don't fuel you, why does eating no fruit or veg make a person ill (e.g. scurvy); is any food 'all bad' or does it depend on how much; and why can't you live without water even though it gives zero energy.
activities.insight: In a fair comparison of equal masses, energy-dense foods (fatty/starchy and low in water) usually release far more measurable heat than watery foods. This challenges the idea that all healthy foods supply lots of energy and locates most dietary energy in carbohydrates and lipids.

activities.title: Check and apply: nutrient roles and energy
steps: Match each nutrient to its main job (e.g. 'which nutrient is mainly for growth and repair?' → protein).
Categorise each of the seven nutrients as 'provides energy' or 'no energy', treating protein as an energy source only in its backup role.

Respond to a real-world claim, e.g. a cereal box stating flakes are 'packed with vitamins for energy' and a friend saying vitamins give you energy to run around: explain which parts of the diet actually provide energy and what vitamins are really for.
activities.insight: A secure learner separates the main energy-providers (carbohydrates, fats) from nutrients with other jobs (vitamins, minerals, fibre, water), understands protein as a backup energy source whose main job is growth and repair, and can justify the split against a plausible everyday claim.

checkQuestion: A cereal box says its flakes are 'packed with vitamins for energy', and a friend tells you vitamins are what give you the energy to run around. Is that right — which parts of your diet actually provide the energy, and if that's not what vitamins are for, what are they for?
checkAnswer: Vitamins do not provide energy. Energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and lipids (fats), with protein used only as a backup. Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts for specific body processes (e.g. vitamin C for healthy tissue, vitamin D for bones), and fibre and water provide no energy either.
